description:
Selected in the eighth round, the undersized but gritty Theo Fleury carved out an exceptional NHL career, tallying 1,088 points and winning a Stanley Cup. Starting with the Calgary Flames, Fleury became a cornerstone for the team throughout the 1990s. In a heated rivalry clash against the Edmonton Oilers during the 1991 Stanley Cup Playoffs, Fleury delivered one of the most iconic moments of his career. In Game 6, he intercepted a wayward pass in the neutral zone, using his blazing speed to outrun an Oilers defenseman. On the ensuing breakaway, Fleury buried the overtime winner to force a decisive Game 7. It was the only overtime playoff goal of his storied career.

description:
In a fiercely contested 1988 playoff series against the Philadelphia Flyers, Dale Hunter delivered an unforgettable Game 7 moment, scoring the overtime winner—his second goal of the game—to clinch the series. Breaking away in overtime, Hunter buried the decisive goal past Ron Hextall, putting an exclamation point on the intense matchup. Known for his grit and toughness over a 19-season career, Hunter spent 12 seasons with the Capitals, where his No. 32 jersey now hangs proudly in the rafters in Washington.

description:
Undeterred by his smaller stature, Dino Ciccarelli carved out a Hall of Fame career by thriving in front of the net and battling in hockey’s toughest areas. Starting his NHL journey with the Minnesota North Stars, where he spent parts of nine seasons, Ciccarelli made an immediate impact. During the 1981 Stanley Cup Playoffs, he set a rookie record with his 14th postseason goal in Game 3 of the Stanley Cup Final. The following year, his first full NHL season, Ciccarelli showcased his scoring prowess with an impressive 55 goals and 106 points, culminating in a career total of 1,200 points.

description:
In a memorable moment for the franchise, the Coyotes hosted their first-ever home playoff game in Phoenix during Game 3 of the 1997 Stanley Cup Playoffs against the Mighty Ducks of Anaheim. The crowd, dressed in white for the iconic "White Out," created an electric atmosphere. Late in the first period, with the Coyotes already up by two, Keith Tkachuk capitalized on a loose puck in the neutral zone, feeding Cliff Ronning for a shot that Tkachuk redirected for the team’s third goal of the game. As team captain and a rugged force on the ice, Tkachuk led all skaters in the series with six goals in seven games.

description:

Inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 2001, Gartner’s No. 11 jersey now hangs proudly in the Washington rafters.

A fiery competitor and fan favorite throughout his 20-year NHL career, Jeremy Roenick brought his dynamic play to the Coyotes for six seasons in Phoenix. After recording a hat trick in his previous game, Roenick repeated the feat in spectacular fashion against Patrick Roy and the Colorado Avalanche. Following his snipe and animated celly, hats rained down from the Arizona faithful. Capping a career that included 513 goals and 1,216 points, Roenick was inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame in 2024.

description:
A three-time Selke Trophy winner as the NHL’s top defensive forward, Guy Carbonneau built a Hall of Fame career by shutting down the league’s brightest stars. Over 19 seasons, he captured three Stanley Cups and was a perennial Selke contender. Against the Buffalo Sabres, he displayed his trademark defensive edge with a crushing hit on Pat LaFontaine that forced a turnover and electrified the Montreal crowd. He also contributed offensively, scoring a key third-period shorthanded goal in Game 3 of the 1993 playoffs against Buffalo—a run that ended with the Canadiens hoisting the Cup. Spending his first 13 seasons in Montreal, Carbonneau claimed two of his three championships with the Canadiens.

description:
Beloved in Toronto, where he spent parts of 13 seasons during his 15-year NHL career, Wendel Clark embodied intensity and passion every time he took the ice. In a late December 1989 matchup against the Boston Bruins, Clark delivered an unforgettable overtime game winner. Battling behind the Boston net, he emerged from a scrum of six players with the puck. As it drifted toward the blue line, Clark hustled to keep it in the zone, delivering a hit along the way. Charging to the net, he found a loose puck at the side and buried it, sending the Toronto crowd into a frenzy. Today, Clark’s No. 17 jersey hangs proudly in the Maple Leafs’ rafters.
